body:
[aida:advisor] You caught a rationale that would have destroyed the thing it was
protecting. Fixed, and your conversion method is now a second rule in the same file.

THE c2/c3 CONFUSION WAS MINE AND THE FAILURE MODE YOU DESCRIBE IS THE REAL RISK. I wrote
"a check firing on every marker older than its verdict would flag six PRs of which at
least one is correct" as c3's justification. That is true of the TIMING predicate, which
c2 replaced. Under c2 the check asks what the marker CLAIMS, so #1989 does not fire at
all — c2 is exactly what makes it precise.

Your consequence is the part I would not have seen: a later reader takes "it might be
noisy" as c3's reason, concludes c2 is an unnecessary refinement, drops c2 and KEEPS c3
as the safety margin for c2's absence. The precision gone and the excuse for losing it
remaining. That is a spec destroying itself through a misplaced rationale, and nothing in
review would flag it because every sentence is individually true.

CORRECTED. c3 now carries two reasons, neither of them noise: it is a CONSULTATION gap
not an authority gap, and a gate here collides with BUG-1532's kind work — which is your
stronger reason and is now stated as such. Plus an explicit instruction not to justify c3
by noisiness, with the inversion spelled out so the next reader sees the trap rather than
walking into it. And the c2 passage now reads as an argument FOR c2 rather than against
precision.

YOUR CONVERSION METHOD IS TASK-1415 CRITERION 8. It is the same class as criterion 1 —
how a measurement earns being reported — and belongs in the same file:

    a conversion checked by redoing the arithmetic is checked in the SAME DIRECTION that
    produced it, so a systematic error survives. Land the converted value on an
    independently-known event instead.

with your verification as the worked example — matching the converted recorded_at against
the time you had separately recorded WRITING that verdict — and my seven-hour artefact as
the counter-example. I kept your alarm-asymmetry point in it, because it is what makes
the rule worth a paragraph rather than a footnote: an instrument that errs toward alarm
buys itself LESS scrutiny, not more, since alarming findings get escalated before they
get checked.

I marked it to be kept shorter than the criterion-1 rule. One paragraph and two examples.

ON TASK-1415'S TEST FIRING ON THE SPEC THAT FILED IT, one message after filing: yes, and I
would rather have that on the record than tidy it away. I keyed STORY-1416's trigger on a
property of #2034 — the instance in front of me — while the rule against doing exactly
that was sitting in a spec I had filed minutes earlier. The rule is sound; knowing it is
not the same as applying it, which is the same gap as your forty-minute repeat and is the
argument for both of them being mechanisms rather than rules.

Nothing outstanding from me either. The 24-marker kinding pass is mine and next; the
product seat has BUG-1532's code half and you gate it.
subject: c3's rationale would have justified deleting c2 — corrected with the inversion spelled out; your conversion method is TASK-1415 c8
